title: Finance: Interest and Banking
summary: Banking terms, types of bank accounts, bank statements and fees, and calculating simple and compound interest on savings and loans year by year.

rows: Money taken **out** of an account, e.g. at an ATM.
The amount of money in the account at a particular time.
An instruction that lets a company take a fixed amount from your account each month (e.g. insurance).
An instruction **you** give the bank to pay a fixed amount to someone each month.
Electronic funds transfer: moving money from one account to another online or with an app.
An arrangement to spend more than you have; the account goes into a negative (debit) balance and you pay interest.
The **reward** for saving money, or the **cost** of borrowing money.

items: **Savings account**: keeps money safe and earns a little interest; few transactions.
**Transmission (cheque or current) account**: for everyday spending with a debit card, debit orders and EFTs. Usually has monthly fees and pays little or no interest.
**Fixed deposit**: you agree not to touch the money for a fixed period (e.g. 12 months) and earn a higher interest rate.
**Credit card**: lets you borrow up to a limit; high interest is charged on any amount not paid back by the due date.

notes.text: A **bank statement** lists every transaction in a period. Money in is a **credit** and money out is a **debit**. Each line shows the new balance. Banks charge **fees** for transactions such as ATM withdrawals, card swipes and cash deposits, plus a **monthly service fee**.

notes.title: Worked example 1: reading a statement
notes.problem: Use Thandi's statement. (a) How much did she pay in bank fees in March? (b) What percentage of her salary did the fees use? Round to two decimal places.

notes.label: Saving on fees
notes.text: Swiping your card at a till or using an app is usually cheaper than drawing cash at an ATM. Drawing cash at another bank's ATM costs even more.

With **simple interest**, the interest is calculated on the **original amount** (the **principal**) only, so you earn the same amount of interest every year.

Interest per year = principal × interest rate

notes.caption: The rate is written as a decimal or fraction: 8% = 0,08.

notes.title: Worked example 2: simple interest
notes.problem: Sipho invests R4 000 at 8% simple interest per year for 3 years. How much will he have at the end?

notes.text: With **compound interest**, the interest earned each year is **added** to the balance, and next year's interest is calculated on the **new, bigger balance**. You earn interest on your interest, so the money grows faster. In Grade 10 we work it out year by year in a table.

notes.caption: R4 000 at 8% compound interest per year

notes.title: Worked example 3: comparing the two
notes.problem: How much more does Sipho earn after 3 years with compound interest than with simple interest?

notes.text: When you **borrow**, interest works against you. Loans, overdrafts, store accounts and credit cards charge interest, usually **compound** interest at a much **higher** rate than savings earn. The longer you take to pay back, the more you pay altogether.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Don't forget to **add the principal** back on. The question 'How much will she have?' wants the **total** (principal + interest), not just the interest.
